title: “Mrs. Campbell, your balance is $213,000.”

blocks.text: Before I booked my flight to Las Vegas, I did something I hadn’t done in five years. I went to the cemetery.
The morning air was crisp and biting as I walked through the manicured lawns of Oakwood Memorial. I stopped in front of a granite headstone engraved with a beautiful, weeping angel.
Beloved Sister, Daughter, Friend. Gone Too Soon.

I stood there for an hour. I remembered the day she “died.” The frantic phone call from the Coast Guard. Rushing to the hospital to find David wrapped in a foil blanket, smelling of smoke and gasoline, sobbing uncontrollably into his hands. He told the police that the boat’s engine had exploded. He had been thrown clear into the water, but Chloe had been trapped in the cabin below.

The authorities recovered a body. It was burned beyond recognition. Because Chloe and I were completely estranged from our parents, and because David was the sole witness, the coroner relied on dental records David had hastily provided from our family dentist.
Wait, I thought, staring at the grave. David provided the dental records.

Of course he did. He had planned the whole thing. The body in the casket beneath my feet wasn’t my sister. It was a Jane Doe, or worse, someone David and Chloe had procured just for this sick charade.

I kicked the flowers I had laid there on her birthday just three weeks ago. I kicked them until the petals were crushed into the damp dirt. Then, I turned around, walked to my car, and pulled out my phone.
I didn’t call Agent Miller. I didn’t call the FBI.
I called my travel agent. I needed a one-way ticket to McCarran International Airport.

The Journey into the Desert David thought he was so smart. When he left that morning for his “quarterly western region conference,” he had kissed me on the forehead, told me he loved me, and promised to bring back a souvenir. He told me not to worry about the debt collector. “I’ve got my lawyers on it, babe,” he had said smoothly. “It’s just a clerical error. A mix-up with a vendor. Trust me.”

My flight landed in Vegas at 4:00 PM. I rented an unassuming gray sedan and drove out toward Henderson, Nevada. The sun was beginning to set over the mountains, casting long, bloody streaks of orange and purple across the desert sky.

Agent Miller had left the file on my table, complete with the address of the “business.” According to the documents, Chloe was running a luxury real estate staging company. But it was entirely a front. The company had zero actual clients. It existed solely to launder the massive personal loans David had taken out under my name, funneled through dummy corporations, to pay for their opulent lifestyle.

I pulled into an exclusive, gated community. The kind of place where palm trees were imported and the driveways were paved with imported Italian stone. I had pulled David’s remote access app from his iPad before I left—he used it to monitor the security cameras of our home back in Ohio. He was so arrogant he used the same master password for the Nevada house.
I tapped the screen on my phone. The massive wrought-iron gates swung open for me.

I drove down the winding street until I reached number 404. It was a sprawling, ultra-modern compound made of glass and white stucco. The Porsche from the FBI photos was parked in the driveway. Beside it was David’s rental car.

My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. This was it. The culmination of five years of lies. I parked my rental car a block away, slipping into the shadows as the desert night fell. I checked my purse. Inside was a digital camera, a flash drive, and a heavy iron wrench I had taken from David’s cherished tool box.
I walked up to the front door. I didn’t need to break a window. Using the app on my phone, I disabled the alarm and unlocked the smart deadbolt.
I stepped inside. The air conditioning was freezing, heavily scented with vanilla and sandalwood—Chloe’s favorite perfume.

I walked quietly through the foyer. The house was a monument to wealth. Vaulted ceilings, massive abstract paintings, a sunken living room with a white leather sectional that probably cost more than my first car.
But it was the photos on the mantle that made me stop breathing.

There were dozens of them in silver frames. David and Chloe in Paris. David and Chloe on a yacht in Cabo. David and Chloe standing in front of this very house, holding up a set of keys, beaming at the camera.
It was a professional maternity shoot. Chloe, radiant and heavily pregnant, wearing a sheer white gown, standing in the desert. David was kneeling, kissing her stomach.
I backed away, bumping into a glass side table. It wobbled but didn’t fall. A child. They had a child.
“Mommy!” a high-pitched voice echoed from the back of the house.

I froze. Footsteps padded across the hardwood floor. I ducked behind a massive marble pillar just as David walked into the living room, holding a little boy who looked to be about four years old. The boy had David’s dark hair and Chloe’s bright green eyes.
“Mommy’s getting ready for dinner, buddy,” David cooed, bouncing the child on his hip. “It’s just you and me for a minute.”

A four-year-old. That meant Chloe had gotten pregnant almost immediately after her “funeral.” While I was sitting in my dark living room, unable to eat, unable to sleep, mourning the horrific burning death of my only sister, she was picking out baby names with my husband.

Rage, pure and blinding, flooded my veins. The sadness evaporated. I didn’t want to gather evidence for Agent Miller anymore. Prison was too good for them. Federal white-collar prison was a country club. They would serve a few years, get out, and still have each other.
I needed to take everything from them. Just like they took everything from me.
“He has your eyes, David,” I said, my voice echoing loudly in the cavernous room.
David whipped around. The color instantly drained from his face. He looked like he had just seen a ghost. In a way, he had. The ghost of his actual life.
“Ka… Karen?” he stammered, stumbling backward. He clutched the child tighter. “What… how are you…”
“How am I here?” I asked, walking slowly toward him. “A bird told me. A federal bird named Agent Miller.”
At the sound of my voice, hurried footsteps clicked down the hallway. “Dave? Who is out there?”
Chloe stepped into the living room. She was wearing a stunning black evening gown, a diamond necklace glittering at her throat. She froze, her hand hovering over her chest.
For ten seconds, nobody moved. The little boy looked confused, chewing on his thumb, staring at me.
“Hello, Chloe,” I smiled. “You look great for a corpse.”
Chloe’s shock lasted only a moment before her face hardened into a mask of pure annoyance. Not guilt. Not shame. Annoyance.
“Put Leo in his room, Dave,” she commanded, never taking her eyes off me.
David, shaking like a leaf, hurried the child down the hall and shut the door. He came back into the living room, standing slightly behind Chloe, like a coward using a shield.
“How did you find us?” Chloe demanded, crossing her arms.
“I called the FBI about the $213,000 in loans,” I said, leaning casually against the back of their expensive couch. “Turns out, identity theft leaves a paper trail. Who knew?”
David stepped forward, his hands raised in surrender. “Karen, please. Let me explain. It’s complicated.”

“Complicated?” I laughed. “You faked her death. You burned a boat, buried an empty casket, and then used my name to fund a millionaire lifestyle while you played the grieving hero. What part of that is complicated, David?”

Chloe sighed heavily, walking over to a crystal decanter and pouring herself a glass of bourbon. “It wasn’t supposed to be this way, Karen. I owed some very bad people a lot of money back in Ohio. The kind of people who don’t take payment plans. If I didn’t disappear, they were going to kill me. Dave saved my life.”
“And you decided to thank him by sleeping with him?” I spat.
“Oh, please,” Chloe rolled her eyes, taking a sip. “Dave and I were sleeping together long before the boat fire. Since your wedding day, actually.”
That was the final knife twist. My own wedding day.

“We needed a fresh start,” David pleaded, tears welling in his eyes. “We needed money to set up out here. Your credit was perfect. We were going to pay it back, Karen, I swear! Once the real estate business took off…”
“There is no business!” I yelled, dropping the act. “It’s a shell company! You stole $213,000 to buy Porsches and marble floors while I clipped coupons!”

“So what?” Chloe snapped, stepping into my personal space. She was always taller, always meaner. “What are you going to do, Karen? Go to the cops? The FBI? Go ahead. Dave will get a few years for fraud. I’ll get a slap on the wrist. But we will always have Leo. And you? You will go back to Ohio, entirely alone, completely broke, and utterly pathetic. You have nothing.”
She smiled, a cruel, venomous smirk. “You always were the weak one. Thanks for the credit score, sis.”
David looked at the floor, unable to meet my eyes, but he didn’t contradict her. He had made his choice.
I looked at my sister. I looked at my husband. I took a deep breath, and a slow, genuine smile spread across my face.
“You’re right, Chloe,” I whispered. “I won’t go to the FBI.”
Chloe frowned, her smugness faltering slightly. “What are you talking about?”
“I said, I’m not going to the FBI.” I reached into my purse, pulled out my phone, and checked the time. 7:45 PM.
